title: Key Management & Key Exchange
summary: The operational lifecycle of cryptographic keys, where they should actually live, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and forward secrecy — the practical engineering that determines whether all the cryptography from this group holds up in production.

slides.markdown:
Every topic in this group has quietly assumed a key already exists, is safely stored, and hasn't leaked. That assumption is precisely the part that fails most often in real incidents — nearly every cryptographic failure in production is a key management failure, not a broken algorithm. AES, RSA, and every mode covered so far are mathematically sound; a hardcoded key committed to a public repository defeats all of them instantly.

This closing topic covers the operational side: the key lifecycle, where keys should actually live, how two parties agree on a secret over a public channel in the first place (Diffie-Hellman), and **forward secrecy** — why a key compromised today shouldn't be able to decrypt yesterday's traffic.

A cryptographic key isn't a one-time artifact — it has a full operational lifecycle, and skipping a stage is how keys quietly become the weakest link in an otherwise sound system:

- **Generation** — created using a cryptographically secure random source. A key generated from a weak or predictable seed is broken before it's ever used, regardless of the algorithm's strength.
- **Distribution** — getting the key to everyone who legitimately needs it, without exposing it to anyone who doesn't. This is the exact problem Diffie-Hellman and hybrid encryption exist to solve.
- **Rotation** — replacing a key periodically, even with no known compromise, so that any *undetected* leak has a limited window of usefulness, and so brute-force feasibility doesn't creep up over a key's lifetime.
- **Revocation** — invalidating a key immediately upon known or suspected compromise, not waiting for its scheduled rotation.
- **Destruction** — securely deleting a retired key so it can't be recovered from disk, backups, or memory later.

A mature security program treats every one of these as an automated, auditable process — not a manual step someone remembers to do.

slides.subTitle: HSMs and KMS vs environment variables
slides.markdown:
Where a key is stored determines how much damage a single breach can do, independent of the algorithm protecting the data.

- **Environment variables / config files** — common, and the weakest real option: readable by anything running with the process's permissions, frequently accidentally logged, and a classic source of leaks when committed to version control or exposed via a debug endpoint.
- **KMS (Key Management Service)** — a managed cloud service (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS) that stores keys and performs cryptographic operations *on your behalf* — your application sends data to be encrypted/decrypted and gets a result back, but the raw key material never leaves the service. This adds audit logging, fine-grained access control, and centralized rotation almost for free.
- **HSM (Hardware Security Module)** — dedicated hardware designed so key material physically cannot be extracted, even by someone with full access to the surrounding infrastructure — the strongest option, typically reserved for root keys, certificate authorities, or the highest-value secrets in an organization.

The general principle across all three: **the application should never need to see or handle raw key bytes directly** if it can instead ask a KMS or HSM to perform the operation. Full treatment of cloud-specific key storage is in Cloud Security — the principle here is universal regardless of platform.

slides.subTitle: Agreeing on a secret in plain sight
slides.markdown:
**Diffie-Hellman (DH)** solves a problem that sounds impossible: two parties who have never met, communicating over a channel an eavesdropper can fully observe, end up sharing an identical secret value that the eavesdropper — despite seeing every message exchanged — cannot feasibly compute.

The mechanism relies on a mathematical operation that's easy to compute in one direction and hard to reverse (a different hard problem than RSA's factoring, but the same trapdoor *shape*): each party combines a private random value with a shared public parameter, sends the result to the other party in the clear, and combines what they receive with their own private value. Both sides land on the same final number through different paths; an eavesdropper who only sees the exchanged public values can't feasibly work backward to that shared result.

This is distinct from RSA-based key exchange in one crucial way covered next: because both parties generate fresh private values *for this specific exchange*, DH naturally supports forward secrecy in a way that reusing a long-lived RSA key pair for key exchange does not.

slides.sectionTitle: A Diffie-Hellman exchange, step by step
slides.markdown:
![Diffie-Hellman exchange: Alice and Bob each derive a public value from a private one, swap them in view of an eavesdropper, then each combine the other's public value with their own private value to reach the same shared secret](assets/diffie-hellman-exchange.svg)

The diagram's core point: **the private values a and b are never transmitted**, only values derived from them. The eavesdropper sees exactly the same two public values Alice and Bob exchange, and still can't compute the shared secret, because doing so would require reversing the same hard mathematical problem DH is built on.

slides.subTitle: Today's compromised key shouldn't decrypt yesterday's traffic
slides.markdown:
**Forward secrecy** (also called perfect forward secrecy) is the property that compromising a long-term key today does not let an attacker decrypt *past* traffic that was recorded and stored earlier.

Without it, here's the realistic attack it enables: an attacker records encrypted traffic for years, unable to read any of it — then, at some point, obtains the server's long-term private key (through a breach, a court order, or a future cryptanalytic advance) and retroactively decrypts every recorded session at once. This is exactly what happened conceptually with older TLS configurations that used RSA directly for key exchange: the same long-lived RSA private key that identified the server also, if ever compromised, unlocked every session ever recorded against it.

**Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE)** provides forward secrecy by generating a brand-new, temporary key pair for every single session, used only for that one key exchange and then discarded. Even if the server's long-term identity key is later compromised, there's no way to reconstruct the ephemeral session keys that have already been thrown away — each past session's secret died with the session. This is exactly why modern TLS (1.3 in particular) mandates ephemeral key exchange rather than static RSA key transport.

slides.sectionTitle: Rotating a symmetric key vs an asymmetric key pair
slides.markdown:
| | Rotating a symmetric key | Rotating an asymmetric key pair |
|---|---|---|
| **What has to change** | Every party sharing the key needs the new one | Only the private key holder generates a new pair |
| **Distribution problem** | The new key has to reach every holder securely — the same key-distribution problem this whole group has been solving | The new public key just needs to be published/re-published — no secret to distribute |
| **Trust re-establishment** | Usually none needed — it's just a shared secret | Often requires re-issuing certificates, since a certificate binds a *specific* public key to an identity |
| **Operational difficulty** | Harder as the number of holders grows — every service using a shared symmetric key needs coordinated rotation | Comparatively easier to distribute, but slower due to key generation cost and any certificate re-issuance |

The asymmetry captured in the top row is the real reason rotation strategy differs so much between the two: a symmetric key's rotation difficulty scales with *how many parties hold it*, while an asymmetric key pair's difficulty is mostly about generation cost and re-establishing certificate trust, since the public half never needed to be secretly distributed in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: A hardcoded key committed to source control
slides.markdown:
The single most common real-world key management failure: a secret key, API credential, or encryption key hardcoded directly in source code and committed to version control — sometimes deliberately "just for now," sometimes copy-pasted from a working example and never removed.

This fails catastrophically and permanently for a reason specific to version control: **git history doesn't forget.** Deleting the key from the current file doesn't remove it — it's still recoverable from any earlier commit, by anyone with read access to the repository's history, forever, unless the entire history is rewritten (which breaks every clone and reference to those commits). If the repository is or ever becomes public — a private repo made public, a fork, a misconfigured CI log that echoes the file — the key is permanently exposed the moment it was committed, not the moment anyone happens to notice it.

The fix isn't just removing the line — it's **rotating the exposed key immediately**, treating it as compromised the moment it touched version control regardless of whether anyone is known to have seen it, and moving secret storage to environment-injected secrets or a proper KMS/vault from the start. Tools like pre-commit secret scanners exist specifically to catch this before the commit ever lands, because after it lands, the only real fix is rotation, not deletion.

slides.sectionTitle: Key management as the load-bearing wall
slides.markdown:
Every algorithm in this group — AES, RSA, ECC, HMAC, signatures — is, mathematically, solid. Real-world cryptographic breaches overwhelmingly trace back to key management, not algorithm choice: a reused nonce, a leaked key in a public repository, a certificate that was never rotated after a suspected compromise, a symmetric key shared across far more services than necessary so a single compromise cascades widely.

The pattern worth internalizing for both interviews and real design work: when a system's encryption is described as "broken," the actual root cause is very often upstream of the cipher — how a key was generated, where it lived, who could reach it, and whether it was rotated on any real cadence. Diagnosing a cryptographic incident well means asking about the key's entire lifecycle before questioning the algorithm.

This closes Cryptography. The throughline across all six topics: security is a computational-cost claim resting entirely on a key ([Cryptography Foundations](crypto-foundations)); hashing and HMAC give integrity and authenticated integrity without an inverse; symmetric encryption and its modes turn a key into confidentiality at speed; asymmetric cryptography solves key distribution and, via signing, non-repudiation; certificates and PKI extend signing to bind a public key to a real identity; and this topic ties it all together operationally — a key is only as good as its generation, storage, distribution, rotation, and eventual destruction.

A candidate who can trace any real-world cryptographic system — TLS, a password store, a signed webhook — back through this chain, naming exactly which property each piece provides and where the actual risk lives (almost always in key handling, not the math), is demonstrating the depth this group was built for.
